topic: Optimal Wordle Strategies: An Algorithmic Approach
target_audience: University students with basic computer science or probability knowledge

sections.title: The Core Mechanism: Entropy in Information Theory
sections.content: Introduce the prerequisite concept of 'Information Entropy'. Explain that each guess is a tool to maximize information gain. We view the word pool as a set of possibilities where the best guess is the one that narrows down the remaining candidates most effectively (splitting the search tree).
sections.example: Imagine a 'Word-Detective Bot'. If 100 words remain, a good guess acts like a filter, slicing the group into smaller, equal-sized subsets.

sections.title: Mathematical Framework: Expected Information Gain
sections.content: Define the formula for Entropy H(X) = -Σ p(x) log2 p(x). Visualize this as a probability distribution graph where we aim for a 'balanced' tree structure. A guess that yields many possible color patterns (Green/Yellow/Gray) is superior to one that yields only one frequent result.
sections.example: Visual chart comparing the 'flat' distribution of the word 'CRANE' versus the 'skewed' distribution of the word 'XYLYL', showing how 'CRANE' provides higher certainty.

sections.title: Strategy 1: Frequency Analysis (The 'Vowel-Heavy' Start)
sections.content: Discuss the 'Greedy Algorithm' approach. Why do words like 'ADIEU' or 'STARE' perform well? Because they prioritize the most frequent letters in the English language, effectively pruning the search space by identifying common vowels and high-frequency consonants.
sections.example: A visual 'Heat Map' overlay on the English alphabet showing that letters like E, A, R, I, O are 'High-Value Tiles' for the first move.

sections.title: Strategy 2: The Pruning Technique (Hard Mode Logic)
sections.content: Explain how to refine strategies after the first move. Once feedback is received, the algorithm shifts from 'Information Maximization' (Entropy) to 'Candidate Reduction' (Maximal intersection). Mention the trade-off between identifying letters versus identifying positions.
sections.example: An animation of a 'Decision Tree' where the branch 'CRANE' leads to 10 possible words, versus a non-optimal guess leading to 80 possible words.

sections.title: Application: Simulation and Conclusion
sections.content: Summarize that the 'Optimal' strategy combines high-entropy opening moves with iterative pruning. Challenge students to think about how computer bots play vs. human intuition, highlighting that optimal strategy is about minimizing the 'Path Length' to the target word.
sections.example: A 'Robot-vs-Human' race visual: The robot uses a min-max algorithm to reach the word 'PIZZA' in 3 turns, while a human relies on intuition and usually takes 4-5.
